title: Bodhisattva's Four Methods of Guidance
speaker: Kanho Chris Burkhart and Seishu John Wiley
summary: Kanho Chris Burkhart and Seishu John Wiley take up Dogen's four methods of guidance (giving, kind speech, beneficial action, and identity action), building on a talk Andrea gave two weeks earlier. Giving gets a close reading through the phrase "free giving," with the image of offering patience as dana from inside a traffic jam. Beneficial action brings in the burning house parable from the Lotus Sutra, where a father promises his children toy carts to coax them out of the fire. Identity action rests on a passage from the Guanzi, where the ocean does not exclude water and so is large. Kanho and Seishu close by asking what this practice looks like in the marketplace and open the floor to discussion.

sentences.text: **Kanho Chris Burkhart:** Good evening everybody and welcome.
It's nice to see all of you here.
Tonight Chris and I are going to talk about the four methods of guidance and carry on with the talk that Andrea did a couple weeks ago.
We're going to divide it up.
I'm going to do the introduction and then parts two and four and Chris is going to do number one and number three and the conclusion.
So I want to thank Andrea for the talk that she gave two weeks ago even though she's not here.
It really got me to thinking about how determined to practice Dogen was.
Really pretty remarkable.
As Bob mentioned last week, Dogen went into a monastery at the age of thirteen and he was there for six or seven years and he wasn't satisfied with something.
What he was taught, how the practice was going.
So what do you do in thirteenth-century Japan?
He took the perilous, difficult journey of taking a boat to China.
Some people didn't come back from that.
It was a difficult thing to do.
He spent about five years there.
He had to search for a teacher.
He found one, Rujing.
He studied with Rujing for a couple of years and came back to Japan.

As Andrea talked about two weeks ago, because of political upheaval of some kind, after a few years in his own monastery near Kyoto, he had to leave in the middle of the night with just a few followers.
He again did a perilous, difficult journey this time across a good chunk of Japan into the mountains where he established his own monastery in what is now Heiji.
He practiced for twenty or so years there and wrote extensively.
His practice, he founded a kind of practice that became Soto Zen that we use here and that practice is flourishing eight hundred years later.
It's really pretty remarkable when you think about it that somebody from the thirteenth century did something that has lasted for more than eight hundred years.
So pretty remarkable, his determination to practice.
We are the beneficiaries of that.
Dogen is difficult to read, difficult to understand, maybe easy to read, difficult to understand.
So I spent a number of years avoiding him and I would read Joko Beck and Robert Aitken and Shinmyo Suzuki and all the more contemporary people.
And I found his, when I read him, I felt confused and frustrated.
And nowadays I read Dogen and I'm still confused often but I'm not frustrated anymore so maybe I've just gotten used to being confused.
But it's hard to put into words but I find that when I read him now, even when I'm confused, I feel like my understanding of life and practice stretches a little bit and I like that.
I like how that feels.
So it definitely helps to be in a study group, you know, to have other people to talk with if you're studying Dogen or to have a teacher to talk to about Dogen.

And fortunately for me, because of the timing of this talk and our session at Samish, I was able to talk to both Norman Fischer and Michael Newton about some of the questions I had about the four methods of guidance that was very helpful and I'll share some of what they told me later in the talk.
And I also reviewed my notes from the book *Realizing Genjokoan* by Shohaku Okumura.
And as Andrea mentioned two weeks ago, he's really a good source of information about Dogen.
He's studied Dogen for probably fifty years now.
And his book on *Realizing Genjokoan* is really well written.
It's the clearest writing on Dogen I've ever come across.
So very happy to have discovered that.
So that's the introduction for this talk and let me turn it over now to Chris for her part.
Thank you.

I also want to thank Andrea, especially considering that there are seventy-five classicals in *Shobogenzo* and Dogen had several other pieces of writing that we both picked the same one independently of each other.
That was kind of interesting.
And fortunately, giving is something we could talk about for the rest of the year and we would just scratch the surface.
So this is what Dogen says about the first method of guidance.
Giving means non-greet.
Non-greet means not to covet.
Not to covet means not to curry favor.
Even if you govern the four continents, you should always convey the correct teaching with non-greet.

It is to give away unneeded belongings to someone you don't know, to offer flowers blooming on a distant mountain to the Tathagata or, again, to offer treasures you had in a former life to sentient beings.
Whether it is of teaching or of material, each gift has its value and is worth giving.
Even if the gift is not your own, there is no reason to keep from giving.
The question is not whether the gift is valuable, but whether there is merit.
So I looked at several translations and some of them used the words free giving instead of giving.
And I thought that was interesting.
The change made me realize that much giving is not free.
It has strings attached.
It has expectations attached.
So free giving, what does that mean?
Well, let's talk for a while what free giving is not.
Have you ever heard the phrase cold as charity?
The irony of showing the coldness of so-called charity, which should be naturally warm, an inclusive strike straight to the core of conditional giving.
The giving that comes from me, me, me, down to the poor souls who cannot help themselves is ice cold.
Cold charity indeed.
When through the act of giving we think we are placing ourselves above and separate in relationship to the receiver, it is not free giving.
It is an act to enhance our self-esteem, to borrow money for image, or when we donate so others might think we are generous.
When we give Donna to our teachers and expect that enlightenment will soon follow, it has the same sticky feeling as the sale of indulgences to Catholics to shorten time in purgatory.
All the rumor and internet confirmation has it that you can get time off in purgatory for following Pope Francis' Twitter account.
Dogen's free giving is not giving something to someone.
Dogen's free giving is reflected in our meal chant, where we chant about the wonders of giver-receiver and gift.
It is non-dual.
And it goes far beyond what we usually consider giving.
It includes teaching, a penny, a blade of grass.
Nothing is left out.
And perhaps, not so surprisingly, Dogen includes our daily, regular work.
He says, making a living and producing things can be nothing other than giving.

How would our daily life change when doing dishes, taking out the garbage, our eight-to-five job, the file memo, building a wall, taking blood pressure, designing a house, if everything became an act of giving, Donna to the world?
Zen practice touches me deeply in its reverence of the ordinary of everydayness.
If I must be a hermit on a mountain to practice, it may not be so useful when I'm stuck in traffic.
But if I can take my patience to the middle of the traffic jam into the exhaust fumes and honking and offer it as Donna, it has true merit.
One of my favorite passages is this.
I'm quoting Dogen: *Buddha said, If you are to practice giving to yourself, how much more so to your parents, wife and children?
Therefore, you should know that to give to yourself is a part of giving.
To give to your family is also giving.
Even if you give a particle of dust, you should rejoice in your own act, because you correctly transmit the merit of all Buddhas and for the first time practice an act of a Bodhisattva.
The mind of a sentient being is difficult to change.
You should keep on changing the minds of sentient beings from the first moment that they have one particle to the moment that they attain the way.
This should be started by giving.
For this reason, giving is the first of the six paramitas.
Mind is beyond measure.
Things given are beyond measure.
Moreover, in giving, mind transforms the gift and the gift transforms mind.
This is the first method of guidance.*
So the second one is kind speech.

And one of the things that Norman Fischer said in our discussion at Samish about this writing is that Zen practice is basically about human kindness, you know, finding it in ourselves, developing it, and bringing it into the world.
And it also includes kindness for ourselves and not just for people we know and love.
It's even more important to be kind to people who are having difficult lives and may be difficult to relate to.
When you think about it, they need kindness more than anybody.

And the four methods of guidance are not only recommendations about how to relate to others, but they're also intended to inspire anyone who sees these methods in action, to take up the practice, to come to the Dharma, designed to try to attract people to follow the Dharma.
And I think we can relate to that, you know, seeing someone handle a situation really beautifully, really well is inspiring.
And it does make one want to, oh, you know, I'd like to be like that.
I bet we all have examples in our lives of seeing someone handle something really skillfully and wanting to copy that.
A sentence from this kind speech section which I'm going to discuss now says, and this is Dogen: *Those who hear of your kind speech will be deeply touched, they will never forget it.*
So this is what he means by influencing people who might see your actions in the world.
And the kind speech section is very straightforward.
The first sentence says, again, quoting Dogen, kind speech means that when you see sentient beings, you arouse the mind of compassion and offer words of loving care.
It is contrary to cruel or violent speech.
So immediately, the importance of our state of mind is mentioned.
Spoken words are not the only important thing.
The condition of the mind as words are being spoken is crucial.
And so now we're talking about developing the mind of compassion.
Near the end of this section, Dogen says, you should know that kind speech arises from the seed of compassionate mind.
And he goes on to emphasize how important kind speech is and to make this effort over many lifetimes.
If kind speech is offered, little by little, virtue will grow.
You should be willing to practice it for this entire life.
Do not give up, world after world, life after life.
Kind speech is the basis for reconciling rulers and subduing enemies.
Those who hear kind speech from you have a delighted expression and a joyful mind.
And here's the sentence I've already quoted: *Those who hear of your kind speech will be deeply touched.
They will never forget it.* You should again, Dogen, you should know that kind speech arises from the seed of compassionate mind.
You should ponder the fact that kind speech is not just praising the merit of others.
It has the power to change the destiny of a nation.
So here we are reminded about how important kind speech is and how powerful it is.
Don't minimize its importance and practice it forever.
The third method of guidance is beneficial action.
Beneficial action at times is also translated as helpful conduct.
Another Buddhist term for it is upaya, skillful means.
Perhaps the most famous passage about upaya is a parable of the burning house, which is in the Lotus Sutra.
A fire broke out in the house of a wealthy man who had many children.
The man shouted at his children to escape the fire, but they were playing games, had no understanding of fire, and did not listen to his warning.
So the father told his children, *Listen, outside the gate are the cards that you've always wanted.
Cards pulled by goats, cards pulled by deer, and cards pulled by oxen.
Why don't you come out and play with them?* He knew that these things would be irresistible.
The children eager to play with the new toys ran out of the house.
But instead of the cards they had been promised, there was only one card pulled by white bullocks.
So this story is interesting on many levels.
First we have this precept of not lying.
And there is the father who lies to his kids.
And it's in the Lotus Sutra and very much quoted.
So what is it about?
So first I should say telling lies using superior knowledge or intelligence that is not skillful means.
That's not upaya.
The creator purpose does not make it fine and dandy to deceive.
The father will still need to deal with the fallout over the lies, the resentment that the children will have over being deceived.
And dad didn't think we were smart enough to get it.
He should have explained it to us better.
*Upaya*, skillful means, speaks to the father spontaneously using the best he had at the time, the best he could think of to save his children.
There was no plan B, there was no time to hatch out the perfect thing to say.
It is beneficial to explain gently the how and why.
And yet, when a child is about to run into traffic, we will grab whatever we can get a hold of and yank her back to safety.
Old Master Guido says that generosity and helpful conduct, or beneficial action, arise naturally when wisdom and equilibrium of body and mind are present.
So he speaks to having trust in our action that even when we don't have time to think out the perfect plan, to trust our beneficial action in case of emergency.
Dogen says something slightly different, actually very different.
Beneficial action is skillfully to benefit all classes of sentient beings.
That is, to care about their distant and near future and help them by using skillful means.
In ancient times, someone helped a caged tortoise.
Another took care of an injured sparrow.
They did not expect a reward; they were moved to do so only for the sake of beneficial action.
Foolish people think that if they help others first, their own benefit will be lost.
But this is not so.
Beneficial action is an act of oneness, benefiting self and others together.
So this is where Dogen gets hard to understand at times, talking about tortoises and sparrows.
We assume that those were fables or stories that were very well known to the people of Dogen's time.
And when he mentions the tortoise and the sparrow, everybody knows, oh, yeah, this was Kongyu who pitied a caged tortoise and set it free, and as a result, attained a high government position.
And Yang Bao of the later Han dynasty tended an injured sparrow who then appeared in his dream, and his family had four generations of good fortune.
So fortunately, there are commentaries on Dogen's fighting, and they shine a little light on these phrases that might otherwise be very confusing.
So the next line is not from a Dogen scholar, so please feel very free to doubt it.
It's my own take.
Dogen, whatever he says, points radically towards awakening, whether he talks about being in a boat or sparrows or tortoises or beneficial action.
He's only interested at pointing at awakening hours.
He's helping us, showing us, guiding us to the point we should see.
So in that sense, I feel whatever he wrote in the Four Methods of Guidance, he is pointing at these acts of oneness, of non-duality.
He's pointing at the oneness of actor, act, and the person or being who benefits.
Just like with giving, beneficial action is missing the heart of the matter.
When I think in a linear fashion, I did this to benefit so-and-so.
And when I add should to the mix, it becomes even stickier.
Then I have an actor, an act, the beneficiary, and a judge, and that judge is probably me.
Action for the sake of should by someone who is unwilling is not free-giving, no matter what the mouth says.
It's a silent movie.
Watch what people do.
So the next sentence is really strong: Thus, you should benefit friend and enemy equally.
You should benefit self and others alike.
Now, there is a whole lot of interesting things packed into one sentence.
Easy to say, very hard to do.
And like so many other things, I may need to train for this.
So maybe I work with my resistance and clinging and self when I undertake beneficial action.
Maybe I work with my self-awareness, my resistance, my mindfulness, and especially with benefiting friends and enemies and self alike.
That is difficult.
It doesn't just happen.
So when we feel that this was not beneficial action or free-giving, we should be very gentle with ourselves and just see what came up, what happened, and then try again.
So if one sincerely engages with this practice, then we see that Dogen's message of non-duality cannot be avoided.
It's it.
If you have this mind, even beneficial action for the sake of grasses, trees, wind, and water is spontaneous and unremitting.
So I did the dictionary thing.
I looked up spontaneous and unremitting.
It means performed or occurring as a result of a sudden inner impulse or inclination, and without premeditation or external stimulus, never relaxing or slackening, incessant.
Am I ready to engage this way?
Am I ready to, as Dogen says, leave flowers to the wind, birds to the season, leaving treasure just as treasure?
Can I live without taking more space than necessary?
Can I leave the environment treasure just as treasure?
The flower on the hillside and yet fully give it and fully engage.
Pretty easy stuff.
This one's even tougher, I think.

The fourth method of guidance is called identity action, and this is a term that translators chose after studying the original Japanese terms that Dogen used and then converting it to current Japanese and then trying to figure out what was he trying to say.
The first sentence of this section reads, identity action means non-difference.
It is non-difference from self, non-difference from others.
Now this is a theme from Dogen's writing, and this is one of the things that Shohaku Okumura talks about in *Realizing Genjokoan*.
So he said that in Genjokoan, the word koan means both the equality of all things, ko, K-O, and the uniqueness and particularity of each and every being, on.
So ko and on are actually in opposition to each other.
Reality or emptiness includes both unity and difference.
The universe is one, no separation, but it's also a collection of unique individual beings.
So that's absolute and relative truth together.
And putting these ideas into daily life means actualizing both individual and community practice.
So that's a personal practice that I perform with my body, but it benefits the whole community.
And this is what Dogen is talking about in the Four Methods of Guidance.
Identity action also means that your words match your actions.
And one of the things Norman Fischer said when I was talking with him about this is that Dogen is saying, when I act, I include everything.
It's in my consciousness.
So that's something for us to aspire to after maybe many lifetimes of practice.
Going back to the text, action means right form, dignity, correct manner.
This means you cause yourself to be an identity with others after causing others to be an identity with you.
However, the relationship of self and others varies limitlessly with circumstances.
So I found these sentences a little confusing, especially the order of them.
To be an identity with others after causing others to be an identity with you, that seems like the wrong order to me.
And I talked with Norman about it, but I also went online and listened to a couple of talks on this bit of writing.
And that was very helpful because there was a discussion that some people had.
And what they concluded was that after causing others to be an identity with you has to do with making sure that other people are receptive to our input.
We can't go around trying to be helpful without paying attention to how our efforts are being received.
And that really makes a lot of sense.
So people have to have some identity with what we are trying to do, or they're not going to want to have anything to do with it.
And then Norman talked about the fact that each one of us, because we're alive today here in this place, we've already received so much.

I mean we have clean water, we have roads, we have somebody built our cars, somebody built our houses, somebody grew the food we eat, somebody brought it to the grocery store, and you could go on and on with all the things that we have received just because we're here.
We didn't do anything for them.
So part of identity action is to pay that back.
So because we owe something back for all that we have received, then the sentence, the relationship of self and others varies limitlessly with circumstances.
And this just means there are many ways to be an example of identity action.
And again, this is the mixing of individual lives, individual action and community and universal, which comes up over and over again in Dobin's writings.
Chris was talking about it just a couple of minutes ago.
Then Dobin goes on to quote a book called the *Guanzi*, which is a book from ancient China written around the seventh century BCE.
And here's what he says.
*The Guanzi says, the ocean does not exclude water.
That is why it is large.
Mountain does not exclude earth.
That is why it is high.
A wise lord does not exclude people.
That is why he has many subjects that the ocean does not exclude water is identity action.
Water does not exclude the ocean either.
This being so, water comes together to form the ocean.
Earth piles up to form mountains.*
My understanding is that because the ocean does not exclude the ocean, it is the ocean and it is large.
Because mountains do not exclude mountains, they are mountains and they are high.
So here Dobin is giving examples of inclusion.
Being open and accepting everything like the ocean is identity action.
Water can symbolize individual relative life and the ocean, the universal absolute side of life.
So here again they're mixed.
Creeks and rivers run into the ocean.
The ocean accepts everything.
Creeks and rivers represent sort of the individual aspect of life and the ocean is the universal.
Then I'll read a couple of sections just to finish here.
*Because a wise lord is not weary of people, his subjects assemble.
Subjects means nation.
Wise lord means ruler of a nation.
A ruler is not supposed to be weary of people.
Not to be weary of people does not mean to give no reward or punishment.
Although a ruler gives reward and punishment, he does not weary of people.
People form a nation and seek a wise lord, but they do not know completely the reason why a wise lord is wise.
They only hope to be supported by the wise lord.
They do not notice that they are the ones who support the wise lord.
In this way the principle of identity action is applied to both the wise lord and all the people.
This being so, identity action is a vow of bodhisattvas.
So this last part is about wise lords, subjects, and governments has to do with accepting everyone.
And even if rewards and punishments are given, that can be done in a loving manner without excluding someone.*

And then he applying identity action to the wise lord and the people of a nation is his way of saying that if the people of a nation have high standards, then the wise lord will have high standards and vice versa.
It's not just the job of the wise lord to govern wisely.
It's everybody's job.
People can't just sit back and say there's nothing they can do.
And then Dogen just finishes to remind us that each one of these four methods of guidance includes the other three.
So there are actually sixteen methods of guidance for sentient beings.
So then I'll turn it over to you.
So this is pretty much the end of the four methods of guidance.
One thing I found interesting was that the title had been also translated as the four elements of bodhisattva social relations or the four methods of human relations.
It's a relatively accessible fascicle.
It's not quite as confusing as some of the others are.
And yet I found it the more I was thinking, the more there was to find.
And I thought, especially after Andrea's excellent talk, well, there's nothing left to talk about.
But it's really incredible how thoughtful Dogen was when he put this together.
What I take away from it is that the four methods of guidance are very interrelated.
I like Thich Nhat Hanh's word, interbeing.
They inter-are.
You cannot or I cannot visualize being able to take one of the four away from the others.
They just together they create a functional model of how to live in this world, how to take our practice out into the world.
So Bodhisattva Shihobo or Shihobo as some call it, transliterated it, speaks to our being practitioners in the marketplace, being a member of society, a member of the human race.
So can we understand this and practice it?
Can we do that?
And what would that look like?
And that is throwing the question out to you.
We have some minutes left.
So John and I thought we should open it to a discussion.
Thank you very much.
